props.title: Caché

sections.content: Michael Haneke's Caché (2005) masterfully weaponizes surveillance footage to create crushing psychological tension. The film follows Georges (Daniel Auteuil), a TV host who receives mysterious videotapes showing his home being recorded. Unlike conventional thriller setups, Haneke refuses to reveal who's behind the camera, instead using the premise to unearth France's buried colonial guilt through Georges' childhood connection to an Algerian boy. The film's legendary final shot - a static wide frame where crucial action happens in the background - has sparked endless debate and represents Haneke's signature style of making viewers work for meaning.

sections.content: The surveillance theme in Caché connects to a rich lineage of films exploring watched/watcher dynamics. The Lives of Others (2006) examines East German surveillance through a Stasi agent monitoring a playwright. Red Road (2006) follows a CCTV operator who becomes obsessed with someone she observes. These films share Caché's interest in how surveillance technology mediates human connection and reveals hidden truths.

Haneke's clinical direction style influenced a wave of European art films dealing with bourgeois guilt and repression. The White Ribbon (2009), his follow-up to Caché, uses similar techniques to examine the roots of fascism. Force Majeure (2014) and The Square (2017) continue this tradition of exposing comfortable middle-class facades through moments of crisis. SUBHEAD: Colonial Guilt and Historical Memory

sections.content: The film's exploration of France's Algerian colonial history connects to other works confronting European colonial legacy. Battle of Algiers (1966) directly depicts the Algerian struggle for independence. Chocolat (1988) by Claire Denis examines colonial childhood memories in Cameroon. Like Caché, these films refuse easy resolution of historical trauma.
